pos: adj. (living, not dead; in Scripture chiefly the report of a resurrection — of a son, of a sinner, and of the Lord Himself)
etymology: From Anglo-Saxon on life, that is, in life — two words worn into one, exactly as asleep, ashore, and afar were. The old form explains why alive can only follow its noun: one says a man alive, never an alive man.
biblical_def: Alive in Scripture is nearly always news, and it is nearly always news that reverses a settled verdict of death. Jacob has mourned Joseph for twenty-two years when the report comes: “Joseph is yet alive, and he is governor over all the land of Egypt” (Gen 45:26) — and the old man's heart faints, because he does not believe them. The father in the parable uses the same word twice for a son who never died at all: “this my son was dead, and is alive again; he was lost, and is found” (Luk 15:24), which is the Lord's own definition of what conversion is. Luke applies it to the resurrection with a lawyer's care: “he shewed himself alive after his passion by many infallible proofs, being seen of them forty days” (Act 1:3). And Paul turns it into the daily reckoning of the Christian: “reckon ye also yourselves to be dead indeed unto sin, but alive unto God through Jesus Christ our Lord” (Rom 6:11) — not a feeling to be worked up but a fact to be counted on.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines alive as having life, in a state of life, not dead — and notes its use for being in a state of action or vigour, and for susceptibility of feeling.
webster_full: ALIVE, a. Having life, in opposition to dead; living; being in a state in which the organs perform their functions.
Joseph is yet alive. Gen. xlv.
2. In a state of action; unextinguished; undestroyed; unexpired; as, keep the fire alive.
3. Cheerful; sprightly; full of alacrity.
Note. From the Saxon on life, in life; hence it is never used before a noun.
scriptures: And told him, saying, Joseph is yet alive, and he is governor over all the land of Egypt. And Jacob's heart fainted, for he believed them not.
For this my son was dead, and is alive again; he was lost, and is found. And they began to be merry.
To whom also he shewed himself alive after his passion by many infallible proofs, being seen of them forty days, and speaking of the things pertaining to the kingdom of God:
Likewise reckon ye also yourselves to be dead indeed unto sin, but alive unto God through Jesus Christ our Lord.
corruption_summary: The resurrection is relocated from history into the disciples' experience — Christ “alive in their hearts” — which is exactly the claim Luke wrote his prologue to exclude.
corruption_paragraphs: Liberal Protestantism from Schleiermacher onward, and the Bultmannian programme after it, has offered the church a resurrection that need not have happened: the Easter faith as the disciples' recovered conviction that the cause of Jesus goes on. Luke forecloses it in a single phrase. He says Christ shewed Himself alive by many infallible proofs — the Greek word means a demonstrable, evidential sign — over forty days, to men who ate with Him. Paul does the same by naming living witnesses and inviting the reader to go and ask them (1Co 15:6). If the tomb was occupied, Paul says, the preaching is vain and the hearers are yet in their sins.

Rom 6:11 corrects the opposite error, which grants the historical resurrection and leaves it in the past. Paul's imperative is reckon — an accountant's word, to count as true what is true. The believer is not told to feel alive to God but to treat as settled fact that he was united to Christ in death and in rising, and then to act accordingly: yield your members as instruments of righteousness. Sanctification in Romans 6 proceeds from a fact reckoned, not from an experience sought.
roots_summary: Anglo-Saxon on life, in life; rendering Hebrew chay (H2416), living, and Greek zao (G2198), to live, and the participle zon, living.
roots_lines: Anglo-Saxon on life — in life; the fused preposition explains why alive never precedes its noun.
Hebrew chay (H2416) — living, alive; the root of chayyim, life, and of Eve's name, Chavvah, mother of all living.
Greek zao (G2198) — to live; “alive unto God” (Rom 6:11) and “shewed himself alive” (Act 1:3).
Greek anezesen — “is alive again” (Luk 15:24), literally lived again; the same verb Paul uses of Christ in Rom 14:9.
Greek tekmerion (G5039) — an infallible proof, a demonstrable token; used once in the New Testament, of the resurrection appearances (Act 1:3).
usage: “Joseph is yet alive” — news that reversed twenty-two years of mourning.
“Was dead, and is alive again” — the father's definition of what happened to his son.
“Reckon ye… alive unto God” — a fact to be counted, not a feeling to be raised.

pos: v. (past of sleep; in Scripture the formula for the death of the covenant believer, and the ground of the word cemetery)
etymology: Past tense of sleep, Anglo-Saxon slaepan. The figurative use for death is not a euphemism invented by mourners; it is the Bible's own vocabulary, and the Greek word behind it, koimao, gives us cemetery — literally a sleeping place.
biblical_def: Slept is the Old Testament's settled formula for the death of a king in covenant: “So David slept with his fathers, and was buried in the city of David” (1Ki 2:10), a phrase repeated of one monarch after another through Kings and Chronicles. The New Testament takes the same word and stakes the resurrection on it. Paul writes that “now is Christ risen from the dead, and become the firstfruits of them that slept” (1Co 15:20) — firstfruits implies a harvest, so the sleepers are not gone but waiting. Matthew reports a startling foretaste at the crucifixion: “the graves were opened; and many bodies of the saints which slept arose” (Mat 27:52). The metaphor is precise, and it is worth attending to what it does and does not claim: sleep implies a body at rest, a waking that is certain, and a person who is not annihilated. It says nothing about the soul, which Scripture places consciously with Christ — absent from the body, present with the Lord.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) gives slept as the past tense of sleep, and notes the scriptural use of sleep to denote death, as of one who rests in the expectation of rising.
webster_full: SLEPT, pret. and pp. of sleep.
SLEEP, v.i. To take rest by a suspension of the voluntary exercise of the powers of the body and mind.
2. To rest; to be unemployed; to be inactive.
3. In Scripture, to die; to depart from this life. David slept with his fathers. 1 Kings ii.
4. To be dead; to lie in the grave, as the body, until the resurrection.
scriptures: So David slept with his fathers, and was buried in the city of David.
But now is Christ risen from the dead, and become the firstfruits of them that slept.
And the graves were opened; and many bodies of the saints which slept arose,
To whom also he shewed himself alive after his passion by many infallible proofs, being seen of them forty days, and speaking of the things pertaining to the kingdom of God:
corruption_summary: The sleep metaphor is pressed into soul sleep — the doctrine that the believer is unconscious between death and resurrection — which the New Testament's own statements about the intermediate state deny.
corruption_paragraphs: Soul sleep, held by the Seventh-day Adventists and the Jehovah's Witnesses and occasionally floated among evangelicals, argues from the biblical language of sleeping to the unconsciousness of the departed. But the figure is applied to the body, which does rest in the grave awaiting the resurrection, and Scripture speaks plainly about the soul. Paul is “willing rather to be absent from the body, and to be present with the Lord” (2Co 5:8), and calls departing “to be with Christ; which is far better” (Php 1:23) — language that makes no sense of an unconscious interval. The Lord tells the thief, “To day shalt thou be with me in paradise” (Luk 23:43). The LBCF states the classical position: the bodies of men return to dust, while their souls immediately return to God who gave them.

The metaphor also refuses the opposite corruption, which dissolves the body altogether into a disembodied immortality of the soul. Greek philosophy was content with that; Scripture is not. Sleepers wake, and they wake bodily — “this corruptible must put on incorruption” (1Co 15:53). That is why Christ is called the firstfruits of them that slept: the first sheaf of a harvest that is of the same kind as itself. Christian burial has always testified to this, which is why the church took the pagan word for a graveyard and replaced it with koimeterion, a dormitory.
roots_summary: Anglo-Saxon slaepan; rendering Hebrew shakab (H7901), to lie down, in the formula “slept with his fathers”, and Greek koimao (G2837), to put to sleep — whence cemetery.
roots_lines: Hebrew shakab (H7901) — to lie down; wayyishkab im abothaw, “he slept with his fathers”, the standing obituary formula of Kings and Chronicles.
Greek koimao (G2837) — to cause to sleep; in the passive, to fall asleep, that is, to die (1Co 15:20; Act 7:60).
Greek koimeterion — a sleeping place; the early church's word for a burial ground, and the origin of English cemetery.
Greek aparche (G536) — firstfruits; the first sheaf, of the same kind as the harvest it guarantees (1Co 15:20).
Dan 12:2 — “many of them that sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake”; the Old Testament's clearest statement of a bodily resurrection of just and unjust.
usage: “David slept with his fathers” — the covenant king's obituary formula.
“The firstfruits of them that slept” — a first sheaf implies a harvest of the same kind.
“The saints which slept arose” — a foretaste at the moment the veil was torn.

pos: v. (to deprive of life; in the sixth commandment, the KJV's rendering of a Hebrew verb that means specifically to murder)
etymology: From Middle English killen, to strike or beat — probably a variant of quell, Anglo-Saxon cwellan, to kill. The English word covers every kind of life-taking, which is exactly the difficulty in the sixth commandment.
biblical_def: “Thou shalt not kill” (Exo 20:13) is four words in English and two in Hebrew, and the Hebrew is more precise than the English. The verb is ratsach, which Scripture uses for murder and for manslaughter — unlawful private killing — and never for the execution of a criminal by the magistrate, for the taking of life in a lawful war, or for the slaughter of animals. Different Hebrew verbs cover those. The commandment therefore forbids the man to take life on his own authority; it does not disarm the magistrate whom God has appointed to bear the sword (Rom 13:4), and it does not contradict the same law-code that prescribes capital penalties a few chapters later. The Lord Jesus extends the commandment inward to anger and contempt (Mat 5:21-22) without loosening it outward. He also sets the fear of man in its place: “fear not them which kill the body, but are not able to kill the soul: but rather fear him which is able to destroy both soul and body in hell” (Mat 10:28). And He names the thief who comes “to steal, and to kill, and to destroy” against Himself, who came that they might have life (Joh 10:10).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines kill as to deprive of life, by any means; to put to death; to slay — noting that it is applied to men, to animals, and figuratively to plants.
webster_full: KILL, v.t. To deprive of life, animal or vegetable, in any manner or by any means.
2. To butcher; to slaughter for food.
3. To quell; to appease; to calm; to still; as, to kill the pain.
Note. The Hebrew word in the sixth commandment signifies properly to murder, and is not used of the execution of justice or of lawful war.
Note. Fear not them which kill the body. Matt. x.
scriptures: And fear not them which kill the body, but are not able to kill the soul: but rather fear him which is able to destroy both soul and body in hell.
The thief cometh not, but for to steal, and to kill, and to destroy: I am come that they might have life, and that they might have it more abundantly.
A time to kill, and a time to heal; a time to break down, and a time to build up;
corruption_summary: “Thou shalt not kill” is quoted flatly against capital punishment and lawful defence, while the same six words are treated as inapplicable to the unborn.
corruption_paragraphs: The pacifist and abolitionist use of Exo 20:13 rests entirely on the breadth of an English verb. The Hebrew ratsach is the language of unlawful private killing; the Torah that gives the commandment also commands the death penalty for murder in the very next chapter, and grounds it in Gen 9:6 on the image of God in the victim. Rom 13:4 says the magistrate bears the sword as the minister of God, a revenger to execute wrath. To read the sixth commandment as forbidding what the same law requires is to make Scripture contradict itself within a page.

The far graver corruption runs the other way. The commandment's actual target — the taking of innocent human life by private hands — describes abortion exactly, and the argument that the unborn child is not yet a neighbour collapses against the Bible's own account of that child: knit together in the womb (Psa 139:13-16), known and sanctified before birth (Jer 1:5), leaping in his mother's womb at the greeting of Mary (Luk 1:41). Exo 21:22-25 assigns penalties for harm done to a woman with child. A culture that reads the sixth commandment as forbidding the execution of a convicted murderer and permitting the destruction of an unborn child has inverted it at both ends.
roots_summary: Middle English killen, to strike; rendering Hebrew ratsach (H7523), to murder or slay unlawfully, distinct from harag, to slay, and shachat, to slaughter for sacrifice; Greek apokteino (G615), to kill.
roots_lines: Hebrew ratsach (H7523) — to murder; the verb of the sixth commandment, used of murder and manslaughter, never of judicial execution or lawful war.
Hebrew harag (H2026) — to slay, kill; the general verb, used of killing in battle and of judicial death.
Hebrew shachat (H7819) — to slaughter, as a sacrificial victim; the altar's verb.
Hebrew muth (H4191) in the causative — to put to death; the verb of the death penalty in the statutes.
Greek apokteino (G615) — to kill, put to death; Mat 10:28, where the body may be killed and the soul cannot.
usage: “Thou shalt not kill” — Hebrew ratsach, unlawful private killing.
“Kill the body… not able to kill the soul” — the limit of what any persecutor can reach.
“A time to kill, and a time to heal” — the Preacher's catalogue of appointed seasons.

pos: v. (past of hang; in the Law the public exposure of an executed body under the curse of God — the statute Paul applies to the cross)
etymology: Past of hang, Anglo-Saxon hangian. In the Old Testament the word almost never describes the method of execution but the display of a body already dead: the criminal was stoned or slain and then hung up, so that the sentence was seen.
biblical_def: The key text is a statute about a corpse: “His body shall not remain all night upon the tree, but thou shalt in any wise bury him that day; (for he that is hanged is accursed of God;) that thy land be not defiled” (Deu 21:23). Two things are legislated at once — the public display of the curse, and a strict limit on it, since even a cursed body may not be left overnight to defile the land. Joshua obeys the statute exactly with the king of Ai, taking the body down at sundown. The narrative books use the word for judicial and poetic reversals: “they hanged Haman on the gallows that he had prepared for Mordecai” (Est 7:10), and Absalom is found “hanged in an oak” (2Sa 18:10), caught by the head that had been his glory. Then Paul takes up Deuteronomy's parenthesis and puts the whole gospel inside it: “Christ hath redeemed us from the curse of the law, being made a curse for us: for it is written, Cursed is every one that hangeth on a tree” (Gal 3:13). Peter preaches the same fact to the council: “whom ye slew and hanged on a tree” (Act 5:30).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) gives hanged as the past of hang when used of the execution or suspension of a person, and notes the scriptural declaration that he that is hanged is accursed of God.
webster_full: HANGED, pret. and pp. of hang. Note. Hanged is used of persons; hung, of things.
HANG, v.t. To suspend; to fasten to some fixed object above, in such a manner as to swing or move.
2. To put to death by suspending by the neck.
Note. He that is hanged is accursed of God. Deut. xxi.
Note. Among the Hebrews the criminal was commonly first put to death, and afterwards hanged upon a tree as a public spectacle.
scriptures: His body shall not remain all night upon the tree, but thou shalt in any wise bury him that day; (for he that is hanged is accursed of God;) that thy land be not defiled, which the LORD thy God giveth thee for an inheritance.
Christ hath redeemed us from the curse of the law, being made a curse for us: for it is written, Cursed is every one that hangeth on a tree:
The God of our fathers raised up Jesus, whom ye slew and hanged on a tree.
So they hanged Haman on the gallows that he had prepared for Mordecai. Then was the king's wrath pacified.
corruption_summary: Penal substitution is dismissed as “cosmic child abuse”, which requires ignoring that Christ bore the curse voluntarily, in union with the Father's purpose, under a statute God Himself had written.
corruption_paragraphs: The charge, popularised by Steve Chalke and repeated across progressive evangelicalism, is that a Father who punishes His Son for the sins of others is guilty of an injustice no human court would tolerate. It misdescribes every party. The Son is not a third party press-ganged into suffering but God incarnate laying down His own life, of which He says “no man taketh it from me” (Joh 10:18); the Father is not venting wrath but executing a purpose the Persons formed together before the foundation of the world; and the sinner is not an innocent bystander but the guilty one whose penalty is borne. Gal 3:13 puts the exchange in one sentence: He was made a curse for us.

Deu 21:23 is what makes the exchange legally intelligible, and it is the reason the crucifixion was such a scandal to Jewish hearers. A hanged man is under God's curse by statute. When Paul cites the verse he is not softening the offence; he is claiming it — the Messiah went deliberately under the sentence the Law pronounced, so that those under the Law's curse might go free. Everything the modern objection finds intolerable is precisely what the apostles preached as good news, and the alternative theories of atonement that avoid it — moral influence, mere example, Christus Victor detached from substitution — leave the curse of Deu 21:23 standing over the sinner with nobody to bear it.
roots_summary: Anglo-Saxon hangian; rendering Hebrew talah (H8518), to hang up, and Greek kremannumi (G2910), to hang, and xulon (G3586), a tree or wooden stake.
roots_lines: Hebrew talah (H8518) — to hang up, suspend; used of displaying an executed body (Deu 21:22-23; Josh 8:29).
Hebrew qelalath elohim — “the curse of God” in Deu 21:23; the hanged man is under a divine, not merely a civil, sentence.
Greek kremannumi (G2910) — to hang; epikataratos pas ho kremamenos epi xulou, “cursed is every one that hangeth on a tree” (Gal 3:13).
Greek xulon (G3586) — wood, a tree or stake; the apostles' deliberate word for the cross (Act 5:30; 10:39; 1Pe 2:24), tying Calvary to Deu 21:23.
Greek katara (G2671) — a curse; Christ is not merely cursed but made a curse, the abstract for the concrete.
usage: “He that is hanged is accursed of God” — a statute, and the reason the cross was a scandal.
“Cursed is every one that hangeth on a tree” — Paul claims the offence rather than softening it.
“Hanged Haman on the gallows that he had prepared” — the reversal that runs through Esther.

pos: v. (past of sell; in Scripture the word for a brother betrayed, a birthright squandered, and a man under sin)
etymology: Past tense of sell, Anglo-Saxon sellan, which originally meant simply to give or hand over — the commercial sense came later. The older meaning survives in the Bible's uses, where what is sold is very often handed over rather than traded.
biblical_def: Sold marks the Bible's worst bargains and its best. The worst are three. Esau “sold his birthright unto Jacob” (Gen 25:33) for a meal, and Hebrews calls him a profane person for it. Joseph's brothers “sold Joseph to the Ishmeelites for twenty pieces of silver” (Gen 37:28) — and Joseph himself later names the providence over it without excusing the crime: ye thought evil, but God meant it unto good. And Paul describes the natural condition of every man under the law: “I am carnal, sold under sin” (Rom 7:14) — not a customer of sin but a slave sold into it, which is why the remedy has to be redemption and not reform. Against these stands the best bargain in Scripture, made by a merchant who knew what he had found: “when he had found one pearl of great price, went and sold all that he had, and bought it” (Mat 13:46) — a man who liquidates everything and counts it no loss.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) gives sold as the past tense and participle of sell, and defines sell as to transfer property to another for an equivalent in money — noting the Scripture use of being sold under sin.
webster_full: SOLD, pret. and pp. of sell.
SELL, v.t. To transfer property, or the exclusive right of possession, to another for an equivalent in money.
2. To betray; to deliver or surrender for money or reward; as, to sell one's country.
3. In Scripture, to give up to the power of another; as, the Lord sold them into the hand of Jabin. Judges iv.
Note. Sold under sin, that is, wholly under its dominion, as a slave sold to a master.
scriptures: And Jacob said, Swear to me this day; and he sware unto him: and he sold his birthright unto Jacob.
Then there passed by Midianites merchantmen; and they drew and lifted up Joseph out of the pit, and sold Joseph to the Ishmeelites for twenty pieces of silver: and they brought Joseph into Egypt.
For we know that the law is spiritual: but I am carnal, sold under sin.
Who, when he had found one pearl of great price, went and sold all that he had, and bought it.
corruption_summary: Rom 7:14 is used to normalise defeat — every Christian permanently “sold under sin” — and the pearl parable is inverted into a lesson about what the sinner must pay.
corruption_paragraphs: Romans 7 has been made into a charter for resignation, as though Paul were describing the settled and unimprovable condition of the believer. The chapter is describing a man under law and without power, and the argument does not stop there: chapter 8 opens with no condemnation and proceeds to the Spirit of life making free from the law of sin and death. Whichever way the interpretive question about Paul's reference is settled — and the Reformed tradition has held both readings — nobody may take “sold under sin” as the last word, because Paul does not. The believer is bought, not still on the block.

The pearl parable is regularly preached as a call to give up everything for Christ, which is true elsewhere in the Gospels but is not what this parable says. The merchant sells all he has because he has found something worth more than everything he had — the transaction is not a sacrifice but an obvious profit, and he goes away richer. Esau in Gen 25:33 is the exact photographic negative: a man who values a thing of infinite worth at the price of one meal because he wants the meal now. Both parables are about appraisal, and the question they put to the reader is what he thinks the kingdom is worth.
roots_summary: Anglo-Saxon sellan, to hand over; rendering Hebrew makar (H4376), to sell, and Greek pipraskō (G4097) and poleo (G4453), to sell.
roots_lines: Anglo-Saxon sellan — to give, hand over; the commercial sense is a later narrowing.
Hebrew makar (H4376) — to sell; used both of commerce and of God delivering Israel into an enemy's hand (Jdg 2:14; 4:2).
Greek pipraskomai — perfect passive in Rom 7:14, pepramenos hupo ten hamartian, “having been sold under sin”: a completed transaction with a standing result.
Greek poleo (G4453) — to sell; the merchant of Mat 13:46 who sold all that he had.
Heb 12:16 — Esau, “who for one morsel of meat sold his birthright”, named a profane person for it.
usage: “He sold his birthright” — an infinite inheritance appraised at one meal.
“Sold Joseph… for twenty pieces of silver” — the price of a boy, and a providence over a crime.
“Sold all that he had, and bought it” — not a sacrifice but an obvious profit.

pos: v. and n. (past of abide; also a dwelling — in Scripture the word for staying put long enough for something to happen)
etymology: Past tense of abide, Anglo-Saxon abidan — a- (intensive) plus bidan, to wait. The root idea is not residence but waiting: to abide is to stay through, and the noun abode is where a man stays.
biblical_def: Abode is a quiet word doing heavy work. It measures the visits that changed lives: Mary “abode with her about three months” (Luk 1:56) — the two women carrying John and Jesus, keeping house together through the first trimester of the incarnation. It measures Paul's method of ministry, which was not itinerant showmanship but settled labour with his hands: “because he was of the same craft, he abode with them, and wrought: for by their occupation they were tentmakers” (Act 18:3). And in the sharpest use of all, it measures the devil by what he did not do: “He was a murderer from the beginning, and abode not in the truth, because there is no truth in him” (Joh 8:44). Satan was in the truth and did not remain there. The whole doctrine of abiding in John hangs on that contrast — the branch that abides in the vine bears fruit, and the one that does not is cast forth and withered.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) gives abode as the past of abide, and as a noun meaning stay, continuance in a place, or a habitation — noting that the primary sense is waiting or continuing.
webster_full: ABODE, pret. of abide.
ABODE, n. Stay; continuance in a place; residence for a longer or shorter time.
2. A place of continuance; a dwelling; a habitation.
ABIDE, v.i. To rest, or dwell; to tarry or stay for a short time.
2. To continue permanently or in the same state; to remain stable or fixed.
scriptures: And Mary abode with her about three months, and returned to her own house.
And because he was of the same craft, he abode with them, and wrought: for by their occupation they were tentmakers.

Ye are of your father the devil, and the lusts of your father ye will do. He was a murderer from the beginning, and abode not in the truth, because there is no truth in him. When he speaketh a lie, he speaketh of his own: for he is a liar, and the father of it.
And he left them, and went out of the city into Bethany; and he lodged there.
corruption_summary: Abiding is recast as a mood to be cultivated in quiet moments, when in John it means continuing in Christ's word and commandments over time.
corruption_paragraphs: Much devotional writing treats abiding as an interior atmosphere — a felt closeness maintained by stillness and technique — so that a believer who is not feeling it concludes he is not abiding. John defines it far more plainly and far more accessibly. “If ye keep my commandments, ye shall abide in my love” (Joh 15:10); “If ye continue in my word, then are ye my disciples indeed” (Joh 8:31); “he that keepeth his commandments dwelleth in him, and he in him” (1Jn 3:24). Abiding is measured in continuance, not in atmosphere, and it is therefore available to the plodding believer as much as to the ecstatic one.

Act 18:3 rebukes a related distortion about ministry. Paul, the apostle to the Gentiles, abode with Aquila and Priscilla and made tents. The New Testament's greatest missionary spent his weeks in a workshop, and its record of that is a standing rebuke to a ministry culture that prizes platform and mobility over long, ordinary presence among people. Mary's three months in the hill country of Judah are of the same order — the most consequential pregnancy in history spent quietly keeping house with a cousin.
roots_summary: Anglo-Saxon abidan, to wait through; rendering Hebrew yashab (H3427), to sit or dwell, and Greek meno (G3306), to remain, abide, continue.
roots_lines: Anglo-Saxon abidan — a- intensive + bidan, to wait; the root sense is enduring through, not merely residing.
Hebrew yashab (H3427) — to sit, remain, dwell; the ordinary Old Testament word behind “abode”.
Greek meno (G3306) — to remain, abide, continue; used forty times in John and twenty-four in his epistles.
Joh 8:44 — ouk esteken en te aletheia, “he stood not in the truth”; the devil was in it and did not remain.
Joh 15:4-10 — the vine discourse, where meno appears eleven times; abiding is the condition of fruit.
usage: “Mary abode with her about three months” — the incarnation's first trimester spent keeping house.
“He abode with them, and wrought” — an apostle in a tentmaker's workshop.
“Abode not in the truth” — the devil was in it, and did not stay.

pos: v. (to depart from; to let remain; to forsake — in Scripture the founding verb of marriage and the promise God gives to the fearful)
etymology: From Anglo-Saxon laefan, to let remain — causative of lifan, to remain. The English verb carries two nearly opposite senses that Scripture uses both of: to go away from, and to let stay.
biblical_def: Leave founds the institution of marriage: “Therefore shall a man leave his father and his mother, and shall cleave unto his wife: and they shall be one flesh” (Gen 2:24) — three verbs in order, and the order is not negotiable. A man leaves, then cleaves, then the two are one flesh; a household is established by a public departure from another household, and the Lord Jesus and Paul both cite the verse as the permanent charter of marriage. The word also carries the strongest negative promise in Scripture: “he hath said, I will never leave thee, nor forsake thee” (Heb 13:5) — and the writer produces it, remarkably, as the cure for covetousness, since a man who is certain of God's presence does not need to hoard. It governs the priority of reconciliation over ritual: “Leave there thy gift before the altar, and go thy way; first be reconciled to thy brother” (Mat 5:24). And in the Psalter it becomes the great resurrection promise, quoted by Peter at Pentecost: “thou wilt not leave my soul in hell; neither wilt thou suffer thine Holy One to see corruption” (Psa 16:10).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines leave as to withdraw or depart from, to forsake, to quit — and also as to suffer to remain, to permit without interposition.
webster_full: LEAVE, v.t. To withdraw or depart from; to quit for a longer or shorter time indefinitely, or forever.
A man shall leave his father and his mother. Gen. ii.
2. To forsake; to desert; to abandon; to relinquish.
3. To suffer to remain; not to take or remove.
4. To have remaining at death; as, to leave a good name.
scriptures: Therefore shall a man leave his father and his mother, and shall cleave unto his wife: and they shall be one flesh.
Let your conversation be without covetousness; and be content with such things as ye have: for he hath said, I will never leave thee, nor forsake thee.
Leave there thy gift before the altar, and go thy way; first be reconciled to thy brother, and then come and offer thy gift.
For thou wilt not leave my soul in hell; neither wilt thou suffer thine Holy One to see corruption.
corruption_summary: Gen 2:24 is treated as a description of ancient custom rather than a creation ordinance, and the leaving clause is quietly dropped from a culture of unformed households.
corruption_paragraphs: The verse is the charter of marriage and both the Lord and the apostle treat it that way. Christ answers the divorce question by going behind Moses to it — “from the beginning it was not so” (Mat 19:8) — and Paul cites it in Eph 5:31 as the pattern of Christ and the church. That places marriage among the creation ordinances, given before the fall, for all mankind and not merely for the covenant community, and it forecloses the modern reading of marriage as an evolving social arrangement whose terms a society may set for itself. One man, one woman, leaving, cleaving, one flesh.

The neglected clause is the first one. Households are formed by leaving, and a marriage in which the primary loyalty of either party has not visibly transferred from parents to spouse has not fully begun. The corresponding modern failure is the indefinitely postponed household — men who never leave, in the sense of never assuming the weight of headship and provision, and marriages contracted without the public break that Gen 2:24 assumes. Heb 13:5 is the promise that makes the leaving possible: a man may let go of every other security because the One who says I will never leave thee does not.
roots_summary: Anglo-Saxon laefan, to let remain; rendering Hebrew azab (H5800), to forsake or leave, and yathar (H3498), to leave over, and Greek kataleipo (G2641) and aphiemi (G863).
roots_lines: Hebrew azab (H5800) — to leave, forsake; the verb of Gen 2:24 and of the cry “why hast thou forsaken me” (Psa 22:1).
Hebrew dabaq (H1692) — to cleave, be glued to; the second verb of Gen 2:24, and the word used of Ruth cleaving unto Naomi.
Hebrew yathar (H3498) — to remain over; the root of the doctrine of the remnant.
Greek kataleipo (G2641) — to leave behind; the Septuagint and New Testament rendering of Gen 2:24 at Mat 19:5 and Eph 5:31.
Heb 13:5 — a double negative of unusual force in the Greek, piling negatives to say I will not, not ever, leave thee nor forsake thee.
usage: “Shall a man leave his father and his mother” — leave, cleave, one flesh, in that order.
“I will never leave thee, nor forsake thee” — produced in Scripture as the cure for covetousness.
“Leave there thy gift before the altar” — reconciliation before ritual.

pos: v. (to come to be; to pass into a state — in Scripture the verb of the new birth, the new creature, and the rejected stone)
etymology: From Anglo-Saxon becuman — be- (about) plus cuman (to come): literally to come about, to arrive at a condition. The sense of to befit (as in it becomes a man) is a later branch of the same word.
biblical_def: Become is the verb of transformation, and the New Testament reserves it for God's work. It states the right of sonship: “as many as received him, to them gave he power to become the sons of God, even to them that believe on his name” (Joh 1:12) — and the next verse rules out any human contribution, since such are born “not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God”. It states the new creation: “if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new” (2Co 5:17). It states the required reversal: “Except ye be converted, and become as little children, ye shall not enter into the kingdom of heaven” (Mat 18:3) — where the childlikeness in view is dependence and lowliness, not innocence, since children are not innocent. And it states the great reversal of the builders' verdict: “The stone which the builders refused is become the head stone of the corner” (Psa 118:22), the verse the Lord Jesus applied to Himself and Peter preached before the Sanhedrin.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines become as to pass from one state to another, to enter into some state or condition — and, transitively, to suit or be suitable to, to befit.
webster_full: BECOME, v.i. To pass from one state to another; to enter into some state or condition, by a change from another state.
The Lord God breathed into his nostrils the breath of life, and man became a living soul. Gen. ii.
2. To become of, usually with what preceding; to be the fate of; to be the end of.
BECOME, v.t. To suit; to be suitable to; to befit; to accord with, in character or circumstances.
Holiness becometh thy house, O Lord, for ever. Ps. xciii.
scriptures: But as many as received him, to them gave he power to become the sons of God, even to them that believe on his name:
Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new.
And said, Verily I say unto you, Except ye be converted, and become as little children, ye shall not enter into the kingdom of heaven.
The stone which the builders refused is become the head stone of the corner.
corruption_summary: Joh 1:12 is read as though the power to become sons lay in the human decision, and Mat 18:3 is sentimentalised into a doctrine of childhood innocence.
corruption_paragraphs: “To them gave he power to become the sons of God” is regularly preached as the charter of decisional religion: God supplies the option, man supplies the choice. John himself excludes that reading in the very next sentence, which specifies that those who so believe “were born, not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God”. Three human sources of new birth are named and all three are denied. The receiving and believing are real and are the believer's own acts; their origin is not. That is the monergism of the new birth, and it is stated by the same apostle who records the Lord telling Nicodemus that a man must be born again to see the kingdom at all.

Mat 18:3 is likewise softened into a tribute to the innocence of children, which Scripture nowhere teaches — “foolishness is bound in the heart of a child” (Pro 22:15), and David says he was shapen in iniquity. The context supplies the actual point: the disciples had been arguing who should be greatest, and the Lord sets a child in the midst and says the greatest is he who humbles himself as this little child. What is commended is smallness, dependence, and the absence of any claim to rank. That is a harder word to the ambitious than a compliment to childhood, and it is the one He gave.
roots_summary: Anglo-Saxon becuman, to come about; rendering Hebrew hayah (H1961), to be, become, come to pass, and Greek ginomai (G1096), to become, come into being.
roots_lines: Anglo-Saxon becuman — be- about + cuman to come; to arrive at a state.
Hebrew hayah (H1961) — to be, become, come to pass; “man became a living soul” (Gen 2:7) and “is become the head stone” (Psa 118:22).
Greek ginomai (G1096) — to come into being, become; distinct from eimi, to be — a distinction John exploits in his prologue, where the Word was and all things were made.
Joh 1:12 — exousian genesthai tekna theou, authority or right to become children of God; exousia is warrant, not raw capability.
Greek kaine ktisis (2Co 5:17) — a new creation; kainos is new in kind, not merely new in time.
usage: “Power to become the sons of God” — a right conferred, and a birth not of the will of man.
“All things are become new” — new in kind, not merely recent.
“Is become the head stone of the corner” — the builders' verdict overturned.

pos: n. (a created thing; in Scripture the whole made order groaning under the curse, and the new creature made in Christ)
etymology: From Latin creatura, a thing created, from creare, to create. The word is a permanent confession: nothing that bears the name creature can be self-existent, and the creature/Creator distinction is the most basic division in the Christian view of reality.
biblical_def: Creature in the Authorized Version means anything God has made, and it carries the doctrine of creation in its very form. It covers the animal order: “Let the earth bring forth the living creature after his kind” (Gen 1:24), where the repeated after his kind fixes the boundaries of the created orders. It covers the whole subjected cosmos: “the earnest expectation of the creature waiteth for the manifestation of the sons of God” (Rom 8:19), and Paul adds that “the whole creation groaneth and travaileth in pain together until now” (Rom 8:22) — the material world is not disposable scenery but a fellow-sufferer awaiting redemption. It covers every human hearer of the gospel: “Go ye into all the world, and preach the gospel to every creature” (Mar 16:15). It covers the goodness of what God has made against every ascetic denial: “every creature of God is good, and nothing to be refused, if it be received with thanksgiving” (1Ti 4:4). And it names the believer himself: in Christ, a new creature.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines creature as that which is created, every being besides the Creator, or every thing not self-existent — and notes its application to man, to animals, and to the whole material creation.
webster_full: CREATURE, n. That which is created; every being besides the Creator, or every thing not self-existent.
The word signifies both the animate and the inanimate creation.
2. An animal of any kind; a living being; a beast.
3. A human being, in contempt or in endearment; as, a poor creature, a pretty creature.
4. A person who owes his rise and fortune to another; a dependant.
scriptures: And God said, Let the earth bring forth the living creature after his kind, cattle, and creeping thing, and beast of the earth after his kind: and it was so.
For the earnest expectation of the creature waiteth for the manifestation of the sons of God.
And he said unto them, Go ye into all the world, and preach the gospel to every creature.
For every creature of God is good, and nothing to be refused, if it be received with thanksgiving:
corruption_summary: The creature is worshipped in the place of the Creator — in the older paganism by name, in the modern version by treating nature as ultimate and man as merely one animal among many.
corruption_paragraphs: Paul's account of the fall of the nations turns on this exact exchange: men “worshipped and served the creature more than the Creator, who is blessed for ever” (Rom 1:25). The modern form rarely builds shrines. It appears instead as a naturalism that grants the material order the properties of God — self-existence, ultimacy, the power to explain itself — and as a deep-ecology sentiment that treats humanity as a blight upon a sacred earth. Gen 1:24-28 rules out both: the creature is made, it is made after its kind, it is good, and man is set over it as steward and image-bearer, distinct in office and in nature from the beasts.

The opposite error despises the creature, and 1Ti 4:4 is written against it. Paul is answering teachers who forbade marriage and commanded abstinence from meats, and his reply is that every creature of God is good and nothing is to be refused if it is received with thanksgiving. Asceticism that treats the material as inherently defiling is not a stricter holiness but a denial of creation, and it has recurred from the Gnostics through medieval monasticism to modern legalisms about food and pleasure. Rom 8:19-22 completes the picture: the creature is not to be worshipped and not to be despised, but groans with us, and will be delivered with us.
roots_summary: Latin creatura, from creare; rendering Hebrew nephesh chayyah (H5315 with H2416), living soul or creature, and Greek ktisis (G2937) and ktisma (G2938), a thing created.
roots_lines: Latin creatura — a thing created; the word itself confesses that its subject is not self-existent.
Hebrew nephesh chayyah — living creature, living soul; used of the animals in Gen 1:24 and of man in Gen 2:7.
Hebrew min (H4327) — kind, species; the repeated “after his kind” that bounds the created orders.
Greek ktisis (G2937) — creation, creature; the groaning creation of Rom 8:19-22 and the “new creature” of 2Co 5:17.
Greek ktisma (G2938) — a created thing; “every creature of God is good” (1Ti 4:4).
usage: “The living creature after his kind” — created orders with fixed boundaries.
“The earnest expectation of the creature” — the made world waiting, not discarded.
“Every creature of God is good” — against every asceticism that treats matter as defiling.

pos: v. (past of obtain; in Scripture what the elect receive and the seeker does not — mercy got, not achieved)
etymology: From Latin obtinere — ob- (toward, against) plus tenere (to hold): literally to hold on to, to get and keep. The Latin carries a note of holding what one has come into possession of, which suits the biblical use exactly.
biblical_def: Obtained is one of the New Testament's quiet Calvinist words. Paul states the doctrine of election in a single line built on it: “Israel hath not obtained that which he seeketh for; but the election hath obtained it, and the rest were blinded” (Rom 11:7) — the seeking did not secure it and the election did. Peter says the same of the church made out of no people: “which had not obtained mercy, but now have obtained mercy” (1Pe 2:10), echoing Hosea's Lo-ruhamah. Hebrews uses it of what Christ secured by His own blood, and the tense matters: “by his own blood he entered in once into the holy place, having obtained eternal redemption for us” (Heb 9:12) — the redemption is not offered as a possibility to be actualised by the sinner; it is obtained, done, held. And the same epistle turns the word toward the believer's daily need at the throne of grace: “that we may obtain mercy, and find grace to help in time of need” (Heb 4:16). What was obtained once is obtained again every morning.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines obtain as to get, procure, or gain possession of, by effort or by request — noting that it implies coming into possession, however the thing is come by.
webster_full: OBTAIN, v.t. To get; to gain; to procure; in a general sense, to gain possession of a thing, whether by effort, by request, or by gift.
That we may obtain mercy. Heb. iv.
2. To keep; to hold.
OBTAIN, v.i. To be received in customary or common use; to continue in use; as, the custom obtains.
Note. From the Latin obtineo, ob and teneo, to hold.
scriptures: What then? Israel hath not obtained that which he seeketh for; but the election hath obtained it, and the rest were blinded
Neither by the blood of goats and calves, but by his own blood he entered in once into the holy place, having obtained eternal redemption for us.
Which in time past were not a people, but are now the people of God: which had not obtained mercy, but now have obtained mercy.
Let us therefore come boldly unto the throne of grace, that we may obtain mercy, and find grace to help in time of need.
corruption_summary: Heb 9:12 is read as though Christ obtained a redemption merely available to all, when the verb says He secured it — the difference between a purchased people and a possible one.
corruption_paragraphs: The universalising reading of the atonement holds that Christ's death made all men savable and that the sinner's faith converts the possibility into a fact. Heb 9:12 does not describe a possibility. Christ entered the holy place having obtained eternal redemption — an aorist participle reporting a completed acquisition — and He entered once, so nothing remains to be added. This is the doctrine of definite atonement, which Owen argued in The Death of Death: Christ did not die to make men redeemable but to redeem them, and what He purchased He will certainly have.

Rom 11:7 states the same principle on the human side, and it is a hard verse for every synergistic scheme. Israel sought and did not obtain; the election obtained. If seeking secured the thing, the seekers would have had it. Paul's conclusion is not that God is arbitrary but that mercy is mercy — “so then it is not of him that willeth, nor of him that runneth, but of God that sheweth mercy” (Rom 9:16). And Heb 4:16 keeps the doctrine from ever becoming cold: the throne of a God who obtains for His people is the throne a believer may approach boldly, and obtain mercy again today.
roots_summary: Latin obtinere, to hold on to; rendering Greek epitugchano (G2013), to attain, eleeo (G1653) in the passive, to be shewn mercy, and heurisko (G2147) with the middle in Heb 9:12.
roots_lines: Latin obtinere — ob- + tenere, to hold; to come into and keep possession.
Greek epetuchen (from G2013) — “obtained” in Rom 11:7; to hit the mark, attain the thing aimed at.
Greek eleethentes (from G1653) — “having obtained mercy” (1Pe 2:10); a passive — mercy is received, never achieved.
Greek heuramenos (middle of G2147) — “having obtained” in Heb 9:12; the middle voice makes it a securing for Himself and for His people.
Hos 1:6, 10; 2:23 — Lo-ruhamah, “not having obtained mercy”, the prophecy Peter and Paul both apply to the calling of the Gentiles.
usage: “The election hath obtained it” — seeking did not secure it; election did.
“Having obtained eternal redemption for us” — secured, not merely offered.
“That we may obtain mercy” — the throne of grace approached boldly, today.
